meta.titre: Metamorphic Rocks and Metamorphism Types: from protolith to grade, facies and texture

sections.contenu_markdown: Marble for floor tiles and monuments, slate for roofing and hard quartzite for road stone are all metamorphic rocks: older rocks that were changed in the solid state by heat, pressure and hot fluids deep in the crust or beside hot magma. Large areas of very old basement rock in Africa are gneiss, schist and granite, which is why a geologist working there meets metamorphic rocks constantly. The GCE asks you to name the rocks formed from a given parent, to distinguish contact from regional metamorphism, and to explain what a metamorphic facies is.

items: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma and sedimentary rocks from compacted sediment.
Temperature and pressure both increase with depth in the Earth.
Limestone is made mainly of calcite, which reacts with dilute acid.
A mineral is stable only within a certain range of temperature and pressure.

sections.titre: Metamorphism: agents, types, textures, grade and marbles
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Definition and agents
**Metamorphism** is the change in the mineralogy, texture or structure of an existing rock (the **protolith**) in the solid state, without melting, caused by heat, pressure and chemically active fluids.
- **Heat** supplies the energy for recrystallisation and new minerals.
- **Confining pressure** acts equally in all directions and increases with depth: $P = \rho g h$, about 26 MPa per kilometre for rock of density $2700\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
- **Directed pressure** (differential stress) is greater in one direction; it squeezes the rock and makes platy minerals line up at right angles to the maximum compression.
- **Fluids** carry ions and speed up reactions.

### Types of metamorphism
| Type | Setting | Conditions | Typical result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Contact (thermal) | narrow aureole around an igneous intrusion | high temperature, low pressure | non-foliated, interlocking grains: hornfels, marble, quartzite |
| Regional | mountain belts at convergent plate boundaries, over large areas | high temperature and high directed pressure | foliated rocks: slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss |
| Dynamic (cataclastic) | fault zones | high directed stress, little heat | crushed rock: fault breccia, mylonite |

### Texture and grade
**Foliation** is a planar alignment of minerals: slaty cleavage (very fine), schistosity (visible mica flakes) and gneissic banding (light and dark bands). **Non-foliated** rocks such as marble, quartzite and hornfels are made of interlocking equal grains.

Metamorphic **grade** is the intensity of metamorphism. From mudstone the sequence of increasing grade is slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss, and the index minerals of the Barrovian zones appear in the order chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite.

### Parent rocks and products
Limestone gives marble; quartz sandstone gives quartzite; mudstone gives slate or, by contact, hornfels; granite can give gneiss; basalt gives greenschist and amphibolite.

Pure limestone gives a calcite marble. Limestone with a silica content gives a wollastonite marble: $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3 + CO_2}$. Dolomitic limestone with silica gives a forsterite marble: $2\,\mathrm{CaCO_3{\cdot}MgCO_3} + \mathrm{SiO_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{CaCO_3} + \mathrm{Mg_2SiO_4} + 2\,\mathrm{CO_2}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked what a facies is, or to outline the facies of contact and regional metamorphism.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A **metamorphic facies** is a set of mineral assemblages that formed under the same range of temperature and pressure; rocks of the same chemical composition give the same assemblage within a facies.

| Setting | Facies and diagnostic minerals |
|---|---|
| Contact (high temperature, low pressure) | hornfels facies, in which temperature rises from albite-epidote hornfels through hornblende hornfels to pyroxene hornfels |
| Regional, increasing grade | zeolite, greenschist (chlorite, actinolite, epidote, albite), amphibolite (hornblende and plagioclase), granulite (pyroxene and plagioclase) |
| Subduction zones (high pressure, low temperature) | blueschist (glaucophane) |
| Deep subduction (very high pressure) | eclogite (omphacite and garnet) |

variantes.nom: Identify the rock and the type of metamorphism
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a texture, a setting or a parent rock is described.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Ask three questions. Is it foliated? Foliation means regional metamorphism (or a fault zone if the rock is crushed). Is it non-foliated and granular beside an intrusion? That means contact metamorphism. What is the parent rock? Calcite points to marble, quartz to quartzite, clay minerals to slate, schist or hornfels.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When depth, density or pressure is given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use $P = \rho g h$ with SI units (density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, depth in metres) to get pascals, then convert to megapascals or gigapascals. Confining pressure depends only on depth and density, whereas directed pressure cannot be found from depth.

sections.enonce_markdown: A bed of mudstone is metamorphosed in two places. (a) Beside a granite intrusion it becomes a hard, dark, fine-grained rock with no layering. (b) In a mountain belt formed by plate collision it becomes, at increasing depth, a rock that splits into thin plates, then a rock with shiny mica flakes and garnet crystals, then a coarse banded rock. Name the rocks and the types of metamorphism, explain the changes, and calculate the confining pressure at a depth of $12\ \mathrm{km}$ (take rock density as $2700\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$).

etapes.action: Identify the rock and the type in (a).
etapes.justification: A hard, non-foliated rock next to an intrusion was heated by the magma without strong directed pressure.
Heat alone causes recrystallisation into interlocking grains and growth of new minerals, but nothing aligns the grains, so there is no foliation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Fine interlocking grains, with no layering, in a narrow aureole around the granite.

etapes.action: Identify the type in (b) and name the rocks.
etapes.justification: Plate collision gives high temperature and strong directed pressure over a wide area, which is regional metamorphism, and the rocks become coarser as the grade rises.
etapes.resultat_markdown: **Regional metamorphism**: slate, then **schist** (mica and garnet), then **gneiss**; the grade rises from slate to gneiss.

etapes.justification: Directed pressure makes clay and mica grow with their flat faces at right angles to the maximum compression, which gives slaty cleavage, then schistosity, then banding.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Foliation at right angles to the direction of maximum compression; higher temperature gives larger crystals.

etapes.justification: Use $P = \rho g h$ with the depth in metres.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Beside the granite the mudstone becomes hornfels by contact metamorphism (high temperature, low pressure, no foliation). In the mountain belt regional metamorphism gives the foliated sequence slate, schist and gneiss, and the confining pressure at $12\ \mathrm{km}$ is about $318\ \mathrm{MPa}$.

items.erreur_markdown: "Metamorphism happens when a rock melts and then cools again."
items.pourquoi_faux: Metamorphism takes place in the solid state. A rock that melts becomes magma and forms an igneous rock; only at the very highest grades does partial melting begin.
items.correction_markdown: Define metamorphism as change in the solid state by heat, pressure and fluids, without melting.

items.pourquoi_faux: Foliation needs directed pressure. Marble, quartzite and hornfels form without it and are non-foliated.
items.correction_markdown: Describe foliated rocks (slate, schist, gneiss) and non-foliated rocks (marble, quartzite, hornfels) separately.

items.erreur_markdown: "Foliation forms parallel to the direction of maximum compression."
items.pourquoi_faux: Platy minerals grow or rotate with their flat faces at right angles to the maximum compression, so the foliation is at right angles to it.
items.correction_markdown: State that foliation is perpendicular to the direction of maximum compressive stress.

items.erreur_markdown: "Contact metamorphism needs very high pressure and produces schist."
items.pourquoi_faux: Contact metamorphism is caused by heat from an intrusion at shallow depth, with low pressure and little directed stress, so it produces non-foliated rocks such as hornfels.
items.correction_markdown: Contact: high temperature, low pressure, narrow aureole, hornfels or marble. Regional: high temperature and pressure, large area, schist and gneiss.

items.erreur_markdown: "Marble is formed from sandstone and quartzite from limestone."
items.pourquoi_faux: The parent rocks are the other way round: the mineral of the parent controls the product.
items.correction_markdown: Limestone (calcite) gives marble; quartz sandstone (quartz) gives quartzite.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the metamorphic rock formed when (a) limestone and (b) a quartz sandstone are metamorphosed, and (c) name the low-grade foliated rock made from shale by regional metamorphism. (d) Arrange slate, gneiss, phyllite and schist in order of increasing grade. (e) State which of the three rocks in parts (a) to (c) is foliated.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Marble**. (b) **Quartzite**. (c) **Slate**.

(d) **Slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss**.

(e) Only **slate** is foliated; marble and quartzite are non-foliated rocks of interlocking grains.

items.enonce_markdown: Assume a rock density of $2700\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, a surface temperature of $20\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and a constant geothermal gradient of $30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{km^{-1}}$. (a) At what depth is the confining pressure $0.54\ \mathrm{GPa}$? (b) Calculate the temperature at that depth. (c) Suggest one reason why the real gradient is higher beside an intrusion.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $h = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} = \dfrac{0.54\times10^{9}}{2700\times9.8} = 2.04\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m} = $ **$20.4\ \mathrm{km}$**.

(b) $T = 20 + 30\times20.4 = $ **$632\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$**, about $630\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

(c) Heat flows out of the cooling magma into the surrounding rock, which raises the temperature beside the intrusion above the normal gradient.

items.enonce_markdown: A limestone that contains some quartz is heated beside an intrusion and forms a wollastonite marble. (a) Write the balanced equation for the reaction of calcite with silica. (b) Using $\mathrm{Ca} = 40.1$, $\mathrm{Si} = 28.1$, $\mathrm{C} = 12.0$, $\mathrm{O} = 16.0$ and a molar volume of $24\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$ at r.t.p., calculate for $50.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of calcite the mass of wollastonite formed, the mass of silica needed and the volume of carbon dioxide released. (c) State why this marble is called impure and describe its texture.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{CaCO_3 + SiO_2 \rightarrow CaSiO_3 + CO_2}$.

(b) $M(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = 100.1$, so $n = 50.0/100.1 = 0.4995\ \mathrm{mol}$. Wollastonite: $M(\mathrm{CaSiO_3}) = 116.2$, mass $= 0.4995\times116.2 = $ **$58.0\ \mathrm{g}$**. Silica: $M(\mathrm{SiO_2}) = 60.1$, mass $= 0.4995\times60.1 = $ **$30.0\ \mathrm{g}$**. Carbon dioxide: $0.4995\times24 = $ **$12.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}$**. Check: $50.0 + 30.0 = 80.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of reactants and $58.0 + 22.0 = 80.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of products.

(c) It contains a new silicate mineral as well as calcite because of the silica in the parent limestone; a pure limestone would only recrystallise to a calcite marble. The texture is non-foliated and granoblastic, with interlocking grains.

items_markdown: Metamorphism is change in the solid state, without melting, caused by heat, pressure and chemically active fluids acting on a protolith.

Contact metamorphism: high temperature, low pressure, narrow aureole, non-foliated rocks (hornfels, marble, quartzite). Regional metamorphism: high temperature and directed pressure, large areas, foliated rocks.
Foliation is at right angles to the maximum compression; grade rises slate, phyllite, schist, gneiss, with index minerals chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite.

A metamorphic facies is a set of mineral assemblages formed under one range of temperature and pressure; hornfels facies belongs to contact metamorphism and zeolite, greenschist, amphibolite and granulite to regional metamorphism.

Parent controls product: limestone gives marble, quartz sandstone gives quartzite, mudstone gives slate and its higher-grade relatives; impure limestone gives marbles with silicates such as wollastonite or forsterite.
Confining pressure follows $P = \rho g h$, about 26 MPa per kilometre of depth in rock of density $2700\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$.
